title: First Sentences
subtitle: Ten short sentences with full audio and glosses. Le roi est mort. La reine arrive. Je suis français. The student learns to read before parsing.
objectives: Read ten French sentences aloud with correct pronunciation.
Apply liaison, élision, and stress in connected speech.
Understand the gloss of each sentence without formal grammar.
Build confidence in reading complete French utterances.

sections.heading: Reading before parsing
sections.body:
The natural method begins with reading and listening, not with grammar. You have learned the sounds. You have read names. Now you will read sentences.

Each sentence below has audio and a gloss. Listen first. Then read aloud. Then check the gloss. Do not try to parse the grammar yet. That will come in Stage 2. For now, you are training your ear and your mouth.

These ten sentences are drawn from real French literature: Racine, La Fontaine, Molière, and later authors. They are simple, but they are not made up for students. They are sentences that a seventeenth-century French speaker would recognize and understand.

sections.heading: The ten sentences
sections.instructions: Read each aloud, then check the audio.

sections.heading: Notes on the sentences
sections.body:
Sentence 1: 'Le roi est mort.' Notice the liaison between 'est' and 'mort': [ɛ mɔʁ], no liaison because 'mort' starts with a consonant. But the phrase is famous; it is half of 'Le roi est mort, vive le roi' — the king is dead, long live the king.

Sentence 3: 'Je suis français.' The verb 'suis' comes from 'être' (to be). The adjective 'français' agrees with 'je' (masculine singular). You do not need to know this yet, but you can hear it.

Sentence 5: 'Nous avons du pain.' The liaison between 'nous' and 'avons' is obligatory: [nuz‿avɔ̃]. The 'du' is the partitive article: 'some' bread, not 'the' bread.

Sentence 10: 'Tout est perdu.' Liaison between 'tout' and 'est': [tut‿ɛ]. This is from Racine's Phèdre, one of the most famous lines in French drama.

items.prompt: What does 'Le roi est mort' mean?
In 'Nous avons du pain', is there liaison between 'nous' and 'avons'?
In 'Elle a un livre', is there liaison between 'a' and 'un'?

sections.heading: Stage 1 complete
sections.body:
You have finished Stage 1. You can now pronounce any French text aloud with reasonable accuracy. You know the vowels, the consonants, the silent letters, liaison, and élision. You have read names and sentences.

Stage 2 begins grammar: articles, nouns, adjectives, verbs. The sound comes first; the structure comes second. That is the Kalopaideia method.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can read all ten sentences aloud without hesitation and gloss five of them from memory.
